task_brief: Day 7 of "Capstone Design, Build, and Test" (unit 5, grade 12) is an investigation on capstone design, build, and test. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 60–90 minutes. The unit is working toward: Build the capstone system to a testable milestone with verified requirements, automated tests, and accessibility evidence. Today's work contributes to that by handling capstone design, build, and test at the investigation or close reading stage, against the unit's wider topics of problem validation and stakeholders, requirements and success metrics, architecture and build increments, and verification and test evidence. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Investigate the complete central input printed in activity_setup for capstone design, build, and test. Work out what it does before deciding whether it is any good: trace its behaviour on two inputs, document the actual outputs, and write a plain-language description of its logic. Then evaluate it — name one specific strength and one specific weakness, each tied to a step you traced, and propose one concrete change with the reason it would help. Use only the printed fictional input; do not probe, scan, or attempt access to any live or third-party system. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about capstone design, build, and test, and it belongs to "Capstone Design, Build, and Test", which also covers separate topics such as problem validation and stakeholders. Close out with this check before you stop: State your interpretation of capstone design, build, and test and the specific evidence that would change it. At grade 12 the bar is portfolio-quality independent work you could defend to an outside reader: intent stated, method justified, limitations named honestly, and revision traceable.

Show the process, not only the result — a trace, test log, draft trail, or commit history.
Complete the check criteria list in this package before submitting.

central_input.title: Inline design brief for capstone design, build, and test
central_input.purpose: Design only for the fictional learner described here; no interview, public post, account, camera, or outside tester is needed.
central_input.fictional_user: Kai uses a keyboard, sometimes enlarges text to 200%, and wants a three-step way to track completed reading sessions without entering a name or location.
required_features: Add one reading session in at most three actions.
Show completion using both a word and a visual mark, not color alone.
Store only a fictional book label and a completed/not-completed value.
central_input.fixed_constraint: The prototype is a labelled paper sketch or local file; it is never published and collects no real personal data.

expected_behavior_and_specification: The response must apply capstone design, build, and test to at least three labelled details from the supplied central input.
Every conclusion must identify the exact row, card, requirement, or scenario sentence that supports it.
The response must include one concrete revision or decision and explain the check that would show whether it worked.
The response must name one limitation or trade-off and explain why the available evidence does not settle it.

execution_method.primary: Paper-first method: copy the short labels, annotate them, and complete the response in a notebook or any notes app. No download, installation, account, or internet access is needed.
execution_method.local_optional: A locally available word processor, spreadsheet, drawing tool, or slide editor may be used, but no particular brand or paid feature is required.
execution_method.check_path: Use the numbered specification and the package test/check criteria as a checklist; a parent or tutor can verify the cited labels without needing subject software.

test_cases.expected: one stated check with an observable pass condition
one limitation, unknown, or trade-off stated without inventing facts

debugging_target.observed_failure: An unsupported answer names the lesson topic but cites no labelled detail and has no observable way to check the proposed change.
debugging_target.target: Replace unsupported claims with evidence-linked claims, then add one pass/fail check for the proposed revision or decision.
debugging_target.passing_change: A reader can trace every conclusion to a printed label in the central input and can perform the stated check without outside materials.

equal_credit_alternative.method: A handwritten, typed, spoken-to-a-scribe, or labelled-diagram response earns identical credit when it addresses the same specification.
steps: Label three facts from the central input.
Explain how each fact connects to capstone design, build, and test.
State one revision or decision and its observable pass condition.
Name one limitation or missing fact without searching for outside information.
equal_credit_alternative.evidence_to_submit: Three labelled evidence links, the revision or decision, the pass condition, and the limitation or missing fact.

test_or_check_criteria: The artifact's behaviour is traced on two inputs with actual outputs documented.
A plain-language description of the logic is written before any judgement of quality.
One specific strength and one specific weakness are each tied to a traced step.
A proposed change is concrete and carries a stated reason it would help.
Only artifacts supplied for this task were examined; no live, third-party, or production system was probed, scanned, or accessed.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Adjust quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode while holding the target constant. Where the target names a specific skill, change how it is evidenced rather than substituting a different skill.
Accept typed, handwritten, spoken, diagrammed, or demonstrated responses; where code is the target, accept pseudocode, block-based, or annotated-trace evidence.
Provide screen-reader-compatible editors, adjustable font and contrast, keyboard-only workflows, and an offline paper-and-trace route for every programming task.
task_accessibility_provisions: Provide a screen-reader-compatible editor, adjustable font size and contrast, and a complete keyboard-only workflow. An offline paper-and-trace route is available for every task here and is scored identically to an on-screen one.

Any model, source, or artifact under study is supplied in an accessible parallel form: text alternative or transcript, described version, and a tactile or enlarged rendering where the original is visual. The learner is never required to perceive the source in one specific channel to analyse it.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never use or require a real password, API key, access token, account credential, private message, precise location, or identifiable image; use clearly fictional placeholder values only.
Keep all security work in sandboxed, simulated, or fictional environments; never scan, probe, exploit, or attempt access against real systems, networks, accounts, services, or people.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify and disclose. The tutor may explain concepts, ask diagnostic questions, and help debug, but never silently completes graded project work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, score excerpt, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting capstone design, build, and test.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile or concrete model, or adult demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for capstone design, build, and test follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for capstone design, build, and test, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to capstone design, build, and test works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of capstone design, build, and test, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking capstone design, build, and test mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply capstone design, build, and test under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on capstone design, build, and test rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
